newsitem.title: UK: UK stays silent on BA /American deal.
newsitem.headline: UK stays silent on BA /American deal.

text.p: Hopes were receding on Monday that the British government would rule this week on whether or not to block British Airways' proposed alliance with American Airlines by referring it to for a lengthy investigation to The Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).
Trade and Industry minister Ian Lang had been expected to make a ruling this week based on the findings of a preliminary three-month investigation by his Office of Fair Trading (OFT).
A ministry spokesman would not say when Lang would make his announcement but confirmed that he left for a week-long visit to Mexico and the United States on Sunday.
When he makes his pronouncement the industry generally believes Lang will give the alliance qualified clearance, provided that BA's home hub of London Heathrow is opened up to competition.
"Whatever Lang comes up with we are doubtful it will be referred to the MMC, simply because a political fudge would be better for all concerned," said one airline executive.

However, a spokesman for British long haul operator Virgin Atlantic said on Sunday that the privately-owned carrier still believes Lang will impose such onerous conditions on the alliance that it won't be able to get off the ground.
Virgin's owner Richard Branson says he cannot believe the deal will not be blocked on competition grounds.
BA chief executive Robert Ayling said recently he was determined that the deal with American should be approved, "but not at any price."

BA and American's plans have attracted fierce criticism from Virgin and several U.S. airlines, including BA's estranged U.S. eastcoast partner USAir, as well as some consumer groups, who all say the combine will dominate the trans-Atlantic market.

Under the alliance, BA intends to coordinate its 244 flights a week from Britain to 22 U.S. destinations with all of American's 238 flights a week from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.
They would also combine their frequent flyer programmes and share flight booking codes to promote their connecting flights on computer reservation systems.

BA and American argue in turn that their deal will lead to greater competition on transatlantic routes because it will only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. allow more airlines to compete in the market by agreeing an "open skies" aviation trade pact.

At the same time they say they must be allowed to combine to compete in the wider market against rival alliances such as that between United Airlines and Germany's Lufthansa for all-important transfer traffic.

British clearance for the deal would still leave BA and American with the task of trying to win approval from the U.S. government, which is in turn conditional on the two governments agreeing open skies.
BA and American had hoped their deal would break the deadlock in government negotiations on open skies, which have dragged on for the last five years.

Talks broke down again in August but there has been strong industry speculation that they would be reopened with offers of a compromise based on what the British government has to say in its competition review of the BA/American alliance.
Opponents of the BA/American deal say that if Britain clears it they will then take the fight across the Atlantic.
"The OFT decision is only the first shot in a long war...it is still very much open in the U.S.," said an official with one airline.

The sticking points in the open skies talks this year have been that American's U.S. rivals want their government to secure some of BA's 38 percent share of runway slots at London's Heathrow airport and also to be given "fifth freedom" rights to fly from Britain to third countries.
In turn BA has refused to give up slots to make room for the competition, saying slots can be obtained and they should be bought and sold rather than confiscated from BA.

But Virgin has also demanded that its British government negotiators insist that the U.S. concedes "cabotage" rights, which would allow British airlines to fly domestic routes within the United States, if U.S. airlines are to be allowed "fifth freedom" rights to fly on into mainland Europe.
The U.S. Department of Transportation has said these counter demands are not a quid pro quo.
